answer: A before-after comparison measures an outcome before a program starts and again afterward, then attributes any change to the program. The trap is that this approach assumes the counterfactual was no change, when outcomes often trend up or down for reasons unrelated to the intervention. In the worked example, county screening rates rose from 45% to 60% over four years, but rates were already climbing 3.75 points per year beforehand, so the pre-existing trend alone would have reached 60% with no program at all.

faqs.q: Why can before-and-after comparisons be misleading in program evaluation?
faqs.a: They implicitly assume the outcome would have stayed flat without the program. When a pre-existing trend, broader policy shifts, or other secular changes are already moving the outcome, the post-program value can be reached with no program effect at all.

faqs.q: What is a pre-existing trend and why does it matter?
faqs.a: A pre-existing trend is movement in the outcome that was underway before the intervention began. If screening rates were already rising 3.75 points per year, continuing that slope produces the same after value, so the apparent program effect may simply be the trend continuing.

faqs.q: What question should replace 'did the outcome improve after the program?'
faqs.a: The economist's question is 'compared to what alternative future?' Attributing change to a program requires estimating the counterfactual trajectory, what would have happened without the intervention, rather than assuming no change.
